fabrications.carrier_title: Smart Trainer Roundup: Direct-Drive Models Compared
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Direct-drive smart trainers have become the standard for serious indoor training. By removing the rear wheel, they give a more stable ride feel, quieter operation and more accurate resistance control than older wheel-on designs. We spent a month testing four current models on structured workouts and virtual races.

The flagship model from the largest brand remains the most accurate, staying within one percent of our reference power meter across every test. It is also the heaviest, at over twenty kilograms, which makes it awkward to move between rooms.

{INJECTION}

The mid-range option impressed us most for value. It handled sprints up to 1500 watts without slipping and its flywheel gave a realistic road feel on flat sections. The compact folding trainer is the best pick for small apartments, though it struggles with steep simulated gradients. All four connect over both ANT+ and Bluetooth, and all support ERG mode, which holds a target power regardless of cadence.

fabrications.carrier_title: Forum thread: How often do you replace your chain?
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Original post: I race and train around 300 km a week in season. My shop says I should replace my chain every 2000 km, which seems excessive. What do other racers do?

Reply 1: Buy a chain checker and measure every couple of weeks. Replace at 0.5 percent wear on 11 and 12 speed drivetrains. For me that ends up around 3000 to 4000 km, depending on the weather.

Reply 2: Waxing changed everything for me. My chains now last two or three times longer than with wet lube, and the drivetrain stays clean. It takes an evening to set up, then it's quick.

{INJECTION}

Reply 3: Rotate between two or three chains. Swap them every 1000 km so they wear evenly with the cassette and chainrings. That way you don't need a new cassette every time you change a chain.

Reply 4: Winter grit is the real killer. I run a cheaper chain from November to March and keep the good one for race season.

Firmware 7.2 is now available for all current GPS cycling computers in the range. Install it through the companion phone app or by connecting the device to a computer.

New features: Climb preview now shows gradient for the next 500 metres on any saved route, including unplanned climbs detected from map data. A new workout screen shows target and current power side by side with larger digits. Group ride tracking now supports up to 30 riders.

{INJECTION}

Improvements: Battery life in navigation mode is improved by up to 15 percent. Sensor pairing is faster, and the device now remembers up to eight sensor sets for different bikes. Auto-pause is more reliable at traffic lights.

Fixes: Resolved an issue where lap times could be off by one second after a long ride. Fixed a rare crash when importing routes with more than 5000 points. Corrected the display of elevation units for some regions.

fabrications.carrier_title: Fuel Notes: Carbohydrate Intake in the 48 Hours Before a Road Race
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Many amateur racers spend months on training and then undermine their performance with poor eating in the final two days. Topping up muscle glycogen does not require a giant pasta dinner the night before. It requires steady, planned carbohydrate intake.

Current guidance for events lasting longer than ninety minutes is around eight to ten grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight per day in the 36 to 48 hours before the race. For a 70 kg rider, that is 560 to 700 grams per day, which is more than most people expect.

{INJECTION}

To reach that target without stomach trouble, choose lower-fibre options such as white rice, bagels, juice and rice cakes. Spread intake over five or six meals and snacks. Reduce fat and fibre to keep the gut calm. On race morning, eat a familiar breakfast three hours before the start, then sip a sports drink in the final hour. Practise this routine before a less important race first.

fabrications.carrier_title: Block Periodization for Amateur Racers: A Primer
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Traditional periodization builds fitness gradually, mixing endurance, threshold and high-intensity work across each week. Block periodization takes a different approach. It concentrates one main training focus into a short block of two to four weeks, then shifts to a new focus.

A typical sequence for a road racer might start with an accumulation block focused on aerobic volume, followed by a transmutation block that targets threshold and VO2 max efforts, and finish with a realization block that sharpens race-specific speed.

{INJECTION}

The main advantage is that a concentrated load produces a strong stimulus without asking the body to adapt to everything at once. The drawback is that fitness in non-focus areas can slip during each block. For riders with limited training time, a modified version that keeps one maintenance session for each secondary quality works well. Recovery weeks between blocks are essential, and riders should monitor fatigue closely, as concentrated loading increases the risk of overreaching.
